title: Algebraic Expressions Grade 6: Write, Read & Simplify (Free Quiz)
meta_title: Algebraic Expressions Grade 6 Skills + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master algebraic expressions grade 6: write from words, spot terms and coefficients, combine like terms and evaluate by substitution, with a free quiz.
excerpt: The jump from 3 + 5 to 3x + 5 trips up more Grade 6 students than any other topic. Here is the exact order of skills that makes algebraic expressions click, plus a quick quiz to test them.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write ‘5 more than a number’ on the board and ask a Grade 6 class to put it in maths symbols. You will get 5x, you will get x5, and from the back of the room someone will confidently say 15. That last answer — treating the letter as if it must hold a value right now — is the single biggest hurdle in algebraic expressions grade 6, and once you name it, most of the confusion clears. A letter is just a stand-in for a number we do not know yet. Nothing more.

This is a skill-practice guide, not a theory dump. I will take you through the four moves a Grade 6 student actually needs — writing expressions from words, naming the parts, sorting like from unlike, and evaluating by substitution — in the order that makes each one feed the next. Grab a pencil; these are meant to be tried, not just read.

From words to symbols: the first real skill

Everything starts here. An algebraic expression is a mix of numbers, letters (variables) and operations — like 3x + 7 — with no equals sign. The moment you add an equals sign it becomes an equation, which is a Grade 7 problem. For now, we are only building expressions.

The catch is language. ‘A number increased by 4’ is x + 4, but ‘4 times a number’ is 4x, and ‘4 less than a number’ is x − 4 — not 4 − x. Order matters for subtraction and division in a way it never did with the whole-number sums of Grade 5. I make students read the phrase aloud twice before they write anything.

Naming the parts: terms, coefficients and constants

You cannot simplify what you cannot name. Every expression breaks into terms — the chunks separated by + or − signs. In 4x + 3y − 7, there are three terms: 4x, 3y and 7.

  • Coefficient — the number multiplying the variable. In 4x, the coefficient is 4. A lonely x has a hidden coefficient of 1.
  • Variable — the letter, standing in for an unknown value.
  • Constant — a plain number with no variable attached, like the −7 above. Its value never changes, which is exactly why we call it constant.

Here is a caveat worth flagging early: the sign in front of a term belongs to that term. In 4x − 7, the second term is −7, not 7. Students who forget this get every ‘combine the terms’ question slightly wrong, and it is maddening to debug later.

Like terms vs unlike terms

Two terms are like terms when they have the exact same variable part. So 5x and 2x are like terms; 5x and 2y are not; and 5x and 5x² are not either, because the powers differ. The coefficients can be anything — it is the variable part that must match.

A quick sorting drill

Given 6a, 3b, −2a, 7, b, 9: the a-terms are 6a and −2a; the b-terms are 3b and b; the constants are 7 and 9. Sorting like this on scrap paper before combining is the habit that separates students who get full marks from those who lose one silly mark per question.

Combining like terms to simplify

Now the moves connect. To simplify an expression, add or subtract the coefficients of like terms and leave unlike terms alone. Think of it as tidying: you can stack apples with apples but you cannot add an apple to an orange and call it something new.

Take 6a + 3b − 2a + b. Group the a-terms (6a − 2a = 4a), then the b-terms (3b + b = 4b). The tidy answer is 4a + 4b. Notice we did not get a single number — and we should not, because a and b are still unknown. An expression that stays as an expression is a correct answer, not an unfinished one. That trips up students who expect every maths problem to end in a number.

Evaluating by substitution

Substitution is where the letters finally take a value. To evaluate 3x + 5 when x = 4, replace the x with 4 and work it out: 3 × 4 + 5 = 12 + 5 = 17. Two rules save marks here. First, put the number inside brackets while you substitute — 3(4) + 5 — so you do not accidentally read 34. Second, follow order of operations: multiply before you add.

Substitution is also the honest test of the earlier skills. If a student can take ‘4 less than twice a number’, write it as 2n − 4, and then find its value when n = 10 (that is 16), they have chained all four skills together. That is the finish line for algebraic expressions grade 6.

A sensible practice order

Do not mix everything on day one. In my experience with Tier-2 city students who found algebra scary, the sequence that works is: a couple of days translating words to symbols, then naming parts, then sorting like terms, then combining, and only then substitution. Each skill leans on the one before it. Rush the naming step and the combining falls apart.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight-question quiz below covers exactly these skills — translating, naming parts, spotting like terms, simplifying and substituting. Have your child work through it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 6 Algebraic Expressions Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on writing expressions, terms and coefficients, like terms, simplifying and substitution. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Which expression means ‘7 more than a number x’?
questions.explanation: ‘More than’ means add, and the order does not matter for addition, so it is x + 7 (or 7 + x).

questions.q: In the expression 5y + 3, what is the coefficient of y?
questions.explanation: The coefficient is the number multiplying the variable. In 5y that number is 5.

questions.q: Which term in 4x − 9 is the constant?
questions.explanation: A constant is a plain number with no variable. Here it is 9 (as −9, since the sign belongs to the term).
Like terms have the exact same variable part. 6a and −2a both have the variable a.
These are like terms, so add the coefficients: 8 + 3 = 11, giving 11m. The variable stays.
Combine the a-terms: 6a − 2a = 4a. The 2b is unlike, so it stays. Answer: 4a + 2b.

questions.q: Write ‘4 less than twice a number n’ as an expression.
questions.explanation: Twice a number is 2n, and ‘4 less than’ subtracts 4 from it: 2n − 4.

faq.q: What is an algebraic expression in Grade 6?
faq.a: It is a combination of numbers, variables (letters) and operations, such as 3x + 7, with no equals sign. If it had an equals sign it would be an equation. In Grade 6 the focus is on building and simplifying expressions, not solving equations.

faq.q: What is the difference between a term and a coefficient?
faq.a: A term is a chunk of the expression separated by + or − signs — in 4x + 3y − 7 the terms are 4x, 3y and 7. A coefficient is only the number that multiplies a variable, so in the term 4x the coefficient is 4.

faq.q: How do you know if two terms are like terms?
faq.a: They must have the exact same variable part, including the same power. So 5x and 2x are like terms, but 5x and 2y are not, and neither are 5x and 5x². Only the coefficients are allowed to differ.

faq.q: How do you evaluate an expression by substitution?
faq.a: Replace each variable with its given number, then work it out using order of operations. For 3x + 5 when x = 4, write 3(4) + 5, multiply first to get 12 + 5, and the value is 17.
